extracted.intended_audience: scholars and practitioners of journalism and media studies; students and readers interested in news production, media industry, and consumption patterns
extracted.subtask_description: A mixed-methods empirical study of how monitoring and imitation among journalists (especially in hard news) produce homogenized news products and shape workplace news consumption, with cases from Argentina and comparisons to the United States. The book identifies production, product, and consumption dimensions and their political/cultural implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogenization of the news
rubrics_metrics.description: Rival news organizations can now keep tabs on the competition and imitate them, resulting in a decrease in the diversity of the news; a spiral of sameness and powerlessness with important cultural and political implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should assess the extent to which imitation across outlets reduces content diversity, produces generic news content, and creates field-level effects; consider journalists' and consumers' negative assessments and feelings of powerlessness as part of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring practices and reliance on technology
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a greater intensity and pervasiveness in the monitoring practices and a larger reliance on technology among journalists who produce hard news than among their soft-news counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure monitoring intensity and technological infrastructure use; note that hard-news journalists use information learned through monitoring to imitate other players significantly more than soft-news colleagues, and that monitoring/imitation can manifest differently in online versus print newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent logics of hard- and soft-news production
rubrics_metrics.description: Major differences exist between units devoted to the production of hard and soft news, contrary to strains of literature that blur their boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing newsroom practices or content, distinguish hard- and soft-news production logics—expect higher prevalence of monitoring/imitation in hard news and different organizational practices and outcomes across the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content overlap as evidence of homogenization
rubrics_metrics.description: All cases of content overlap in the print newspapers and nearly all in the online newspapers had to do with hard news; this indicates homogenization of print products over time and strong evidence for homogeneity of both print and online news in the contemporary context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize and quantify content overlap (across multiple levels of analysis) to document homogenization; pay special attention to hard-news beats and longitudinal trends showing increasing overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption patterns at work — ‘readable Web’ predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Online news consumption at work is marked by the prevalence of the 'readable Web': people are far more focused on obtaining information from news sites than on taking advantage of the 'writable Web' (blogs, forums, commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess workplace news routines for displacement from traditional to digital media, emergence of habitual online consumption, and the balance between passive reading and participatory behaviors; sequence and dynamics of consumption matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence between consumer choices and journalistic supply
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between the stories consumers most frequently choose to read and the top stories provided to them by journalists: consumers show lower content-overlap among chosen stories and different thematic selection patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both supply (editorial top stories) and demand (what consumers click/read) to capture divergence; include measures of consumer affect (many dislike homogenized news) and whether negative assessments translate into participatory or social-change actions (often they do not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of wire services and third-party providers in agenda-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth in the proportion of generic news content shared across mainstream media and the growth in the role of third-party providers, such as wire service agencies, might drastically narrow the news agenda and concentrate agenda-setting power among a handful of players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing agenda diversity, account for third-party content sources and their share of published material; consider implications for the watchdog role of journalism and shifts in balance of power in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-methods research design overcoming production–product divide
rubrics_metrics.description: A research design that combines ethnographic and content-analytic studies of production practices, the resulting news stories, and how consumers appropriate these stories overcomes the production–product divide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological standards for studying imitation should include data on newsroom practices, content analysis of produced stories, and consumption patterns (triangulation) rather than studying production or product in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as an interdisciplinary phenomenon (pack journalism, mimicry, herd behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation in news is part of broader social, organizational, and economic imitation phenomena; an interdisciplinary framework builds on communication studies of pack journalism, sociological accounts of inter-organizational mimicry, and economic analyses of herd behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical and analytical work should integrate perspectives from communication, sociology, and economics, and be mindful of technology's role; use complementary strengths of different literatures while recognizing their limitations.
